title: Evaluate the suitability of pork carcasses and organs for human consumption

lessons.title: Identifying abnormalities in pork carcasses and organs
lessons.html:
Why pork evaluation needs care

Pork can carry parasites and bacteria that cause serious disease in people. Pigs are also affected by controlled diseases such as African swine fever and classical swine fever. The meat examiner evaluates every carcass and its organs under the Meat Safety Act 40 of 2000 and its regulations, and refers cases beyond their authority to the meat inspector or veterinarian.

Information to use

  • Ante-mortem findings: fever, lameness, skin lesions, coughing, tail-bitten pigs, or emergency slaughter.
  • Post-mortem examination: head and throat, pluck, viscera and carcass in a fixed sequence, using observation, palpation and the prescribed incisions.
  • Skin and carcass surface: pork is usually dressed skin-on, so skin lesions are visible.

Common deviations in pigs

FindingAppearance and location
Pork measles (Cysticercus cellulosae)Cysts in muscles, often masseters, tongue, heart and diaphragm. Larval stage of Taenia solium, which can cause serious disease in people
Milk spotsWhite scarring on the liver from migrating roundworm larvae (Ascaris)
Pneumonia and pleurisyConsolidated lung lobes; lungs adhered to chest wall
PericarditisHeart sac thickened and adhered
AbscessesOften linked to tail biting, injection sites or joints; may spread through the spine
ArthritisSwollen joints with abnormal fluid
ErysipelasDiamond-shaped skin lesions; arthritis; endocarditis
Lymphadenitis of the submaxillary lymph nodesEnlarged, caseous or calcified nodes; may indicate tuberculosis-like infection
Haemorrhages in skin, kidneys and lymph nodesMay indicate septicaemia or a controlled swine fever: refer immediately
Jaundice, oedema, emaciationYellow tissues; watery tissue; wasted muscle
Scalding and dressing faultsHair, scurf, scald water in lungs, faecal contamination

Always decide whether a lesion is localised or part of a generalised condition, by checking lymph nodes, multiple sites, and signs of fever such as poor bleeding and congestion.

lessons.title: Judgement of pork carcasses
lessons.html:
Judgement options

  • Passed as fit for human consumption.
  • Passed after removal of affected parts for localised lesions.
  • Detained for further examination, laboratory testing or referral.
  • Totally condemned for generalised disease, extensive lesions or unwholesome carcasses.

Applying the principles

SituationDirection of judgement
Liver with milk spots, carcass normalCondemn liver (or trim if mild, as the regulations allow); pass carcass
Localised pleurisy, carcass normalStrip or remove affected pleura and lungs; pass carcass
Tail-bite abscess with no spreadTrim the affected area; examine the spine and lymph nodes
Abscesses in several sites (pyaemia)Total condemnation
Pork measlesJudged strictly according to the regulations because of the human health risk; refer to the meat inspector or veterinarian
Signs of septicaemia or haemorrhagic diseaseDetain, refer immediately and stop movement of related material as instructed
Scald water or ingesta in the lungsCondemn lungs

Suspected controlled diseases

If you suspect a controlled or notifiable disease, such as African swine fever, the response is urgent. Detain the carcass and all parts, inform the meat inspector or veterinarian immediately, and follow instructions. The Animal Diseases Act 35 of 1984 requires reporting. The abattoir may have to stop slaughter, trace the farm of origin and clean and disinfect.

Executing the judgement

  • Ensure trimming is complete and trimmed parts go into condemned containers.
  • Move detained carcasses with their organs and head to the detention area.
  • Ensure condemned carcasses are marked and secured so they cannot be mixed with passed meat.

lessons.title: Completing the task
lessons.html:
Marking and security

Passed carcasses receive the approved inspection mark. Detained carcasses carry detention tags and stay in the secured detention area. Condemned material is marked, placed in leak-proof containers and held in a lockable room until disposal by an approved method.

Records

  • Number of pigs slaughtered per producer.
  • Each condemnation: what was condemned, why, and the carcass number.
  • Outcome of every detained carcass.
  • Suspected notifiable diseases and when they were reported.

Producer feedback

Slaughter findings are valuable information for pig farmers. High rates of milk spots point to poor worm control. Pneumonia and pleurisy suggest problems with ventilation, stocking density or respiratory disease. Tail-bite abscesses point to stress, overcrowding or boredom in the pens. Feedback through the abattoir helps farmers improve health and reduces condemnations.

Line communication

Report recurring dressing faults to the line supervisor: poor de-hairing, scald water aspiration, gut cuts, poor bung tying. These affect hygiene and judgement.

Personal safety and hygiene

  • Sterilise knives and hooks after every carcass and after cutting into lesions.
  • Erysipelas and some other pig diseases can infect people through cuts. Cover wounds and wear gloves where required.
  • Report any illness or infected wound.

Key points

  • Pork measles is a serious human health risk and is judged strictly according to the regulations.
  • Decide whether lesions are localised or generalised before judging.
  • Haemorrhages and septicaemia signs may indicate controlled swine fevers: detain and refer immediately.
  • Secure detained and condemned material and record every decision.
  • Feed findings back to producers to improve herd health.
